questions.q: A man died hours after saying how grateful he was for “a new lease of life,” and his family felt “cheated.” How does the editorial respond?
options: Doctors should have warned him
Not quite. The article says: Death cheats no one; man cheats himself by planning only for this life and not for the one that follows.
Death cheats no one; man cheats himself by planning only for this life and not for the one that follows
Yes. Real new life lies beyond death.
He should not have spoken in public
Not quite. The article says: Death cheats no one; man cheats himself by planning only for this life and not for the one that follows.
Such things happen only by chance
Not quite. The article says: Death cheats no one; man cheats himself by planning only for this life and not for the one that follows.
questions.rationale: “Death cheats no one. It is man that cheats himself. The plans that he should be making for the world after death he makes for this life.”

questions.q: A “Road Closed” sign does not end a journey. What does the article say this teaches about life?
options: When the main route is blocked there are always other, indirect ways to the goal for those who look
Right. Slower perhaps, but one arrives.
One should turn back home
Not quite. The article says: When the main route is blocked there are always other, indirect ways to the goal for those who look.
One should remove the barrier
Not quite. The article says: When the main route is blocked there are always other, indirect ways to the goal for those who look.
One should wait until the road reopens
Not quite. The article says: When the main route is blocked there are always other, indirect ways to the goal for those who look.
questions.rationale: “For every major route which is blocked, there are always several minor roads which are open. It is just a question of having to go about things in a roundabout way.”

questions.q: If you cannot find a place in the front row, what does the article advise?
options: Protest until a place is made
Not quite. The article says: Accept a place at the back for now, until one ahead falls vacant.
Stand in the aisle
Not quite. The article says: Accept a place at the back for now, until one ahead falls vacant.
Accept a place at the back for now, until one ahead falls vacant
Well read. Compromise keeps one moving.
Leave the gathering
Not quite. The article says: Accept a place at the back for now, until one ahead falls vacant.
questions.rationale: “When you fail to find a place for yourself in the front row, you can always make do with one in the rear until a place up ahead finally falls vacant for you.”

questions.q: Faced with a problem, one may take responsibility or blame others. From what does each course spring, according to the article?
options: The first from patience, the second from impatience
Yes. No positive outlook is possible without patience.
The first from age, the second from youth
Not quite. The article says: The first from patience, the second from impatience.
The first from fear, the second from courage
Not quite. The article says: The first from patience, the second from impatience.
The first from weakness, the second from strength
Not quite. The article says: The first from patience, the second from impatience.
questions.rationale: “Whenever one faces a problem, one may either accept the responsibility for it, or attempt to lay the blame on others. The first course results from patience, the second from impatience.”

questions.q: What “very important aspect” of the patient person does the article single out at the end?
options: He avoids making any decision
Not quite. The article says: He takes the trouble to understand the other person’s point of view.
He never changes his mind
Not quite. The article says: He takes the trouble to understand the other person’s point of view.
He takes the trouble to understand the other person’s point of view
Correct. The impatient consider only their own claims.
He keeps silent in every dispute
Not quite. The article says: He takes the trouble to understand the other person’s point of view.
questions.rationale: “A very important aspect of the patient man is that he will take the trouble to acquaint himself with the standpoint of others.”

questions.q: “God is well pleased with them and they are well pleased with Him” (98:8). What does it mean for a servant to be pleased with God?
options: To receive whatever he asks for
Not quite. The article says: To be content with God’s plan of creation and to live by it.
To be praised by other people
Not quite. The article says: To be content with God’s plan of creation and to live by it.
To be content with God’s plan of creation and to live by it
Right. Paradise is a reward, not a purchase.
To be free of every difficulty
Not quite. The article says: To be content with God’s plan of creation and to live by it.
questions.rationale: “God’s servant being pleased with God means he lived his life according to the creation plan of God. The servant was content and pleased with the creation plan of God.”

questions.q: Asked how he found time for two demanding jobs, what did the man reply?
options: “Time is nothing but a function of interest”
Yes. Keenness shortens the work.
“I never sleep”
Not quite. The article says: “Time is nothing but a function of interest”.
“I do each job badly”
Not quite. The article says: “Time is nothing but a function of interest”.
“I have many assistants”
Not quite. The article says: “Time is nothing but a function of interest”.
questions.rationale: “When asked how he found the time to do so much work, he replied, ‘Time is nothing but a function of interest.’”

questions.q: One man completed his travel papers in three weeks; another, with two months in hand, missed his chance. What made the difference?
options: The first pursued the matter with urgency himself; the second grew complacent and left it to someone else
Well reasoned. Ample time is no substitute for interest.
The second lived too far from town
Not quite. The article says: The first pursued the matter with urgency himself; the second grew complacent and left it to someone else.
The first had done it all before
Not quite. The article says: The first pursued the matter with urgency himself; the second grew complacent and left it to someone else.
The first had influential friends
Not quite. The article says: The first pursued the matter with urgency himself; the second grew complacent and left it to someone else.
questions.rationale: “The constraints of time can easily be overcome by keenness and enthusiasm, but… where these elements are lacking, even the least time-bound of ventures are likely to fail.”

questions.q: The Prophet Job lost his wealth and later regained more. What lesson does the article draw from his story?
options: Patience means doing nothing
Not quite. The article says: No loss in this world is final; one who stays patient and hopeful can gain again.
No loss in this world is final; one who stays patient and hopeful can gain again
Exactly. “The Lord gives, and the Lord takes away.”
Misfortune comes only to the careless
Not quite. The article says: No loss in this world is final; one who stays patient and hopeful can gain again.
Wealth should never be owned
Not quite. The article says: No loss in this world is final; one who stays patient and hopeful can gain again.
questions.rationale: “God, being All Merciful, has devised the system of this world in such a way that here no loss or deprivation is final.”

questions.q: According to the saying of the Prophet quoted, which three things continue to benefit a person after death?
options: Continuing charity, knowledge from which others benefit, and righteous children who pray for him
Well read. Everything else is cut off.
Property, titles and monuments
Not quite. The article says: Continuing charity, knowledge from which others benefit, and righteous children who pray for him.
Savings, land and business
Not quite. The article says: Continuing charity, knowledge from which others benefit, and righteous children who pray for him.
Fame, followers and written praise
Not quite. The article says: Continuing charity, knowledge from which others benefit, and righteous children who pray for him.
questions.rationale: “When a man dies, everything connected with him is cut off except three things: Continuous charity, knowledge from which benefit is derived and virtuous children who pray for him.”
